blocks.content: You change one line. Three bugs appear. Sound familiar?
Most developers don't realize the culprit isn't their logic it's their structure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245771201-0dcb7056.png
When a single class is doing too many jobs at once, it becomes a ticking time bomb. Touch any part of it, and the whole thing shakes.
This is what happens when you ignore the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) the idea that every piece of code should have one job, and one job only.
Not because it's a rule. But because code with one responsibility is easier to read, easier to fix, and way easier to change without breaking everything around it.
Let's look at a real example and see exactly where things go wrong.
1. The Problem:

You have probably seen this kind of class before. Maybe you have even written one. It is called a God Class because it tries to do everything, and like most things that try to do everything, it does nothing particularly well.

codes.python:
class HospitalSystem:
    """A single class doing scheduling, records, billing, and dispatch (a God Class)."""

    def __init__(self, patient_name, doctor_id, diagnosis, appointment_date):
        self.patient_name = patient_name
        self.doctor_id = doctor_id
        self.diagnosis = diagnosis
        self.appointment_date = appointment_date

    def check_doctor_availability(self):
        # Fetch doctor schedule, check existing appointments
        print(f"Checking availability for doctor: {self.doctor_id}")
        return True

    def maintain_patient_records(self):
        # Store diagnosis history, update prescriptions, archive past visits
        print(f"Saving medical record for: {self.patient_name} ({self.diagnosis})")

    def calculate_billing(self):
        consultation_fee = 100.0
        insurance_discount = 0.20 * consultation_fee
        final_amount = consultation_fee - insurance_discount
        print(f"Total bill for {self.patient_name}: ${final_amount}")
        return final_amount

    def dispatch_ambulance(self):
        # Detect emergency flag, find nearest available unit, send location to driver
        print(f"Emergency detected for: {self.patient_name}")
        print("Dispatching nearest ambulance to location...")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    system = HospitalSystem("John Doe", "DOC-101", "Fracture", "2026-07-25")
    system.check_doctor_availability()
    system.maintain_patient_records()
    system.calculate_billing()
    system.dispatch_ambulance()

blocks.content: At first glance, this may seem convenient. Everything about hospital management sits in one place. But let's pause and examine what this class is actually doing:
["Checking doctor availability and scheduling","Maintaining patient medical records","Calculating bills and insurance","Dispatching emergency ambulances"]
That's four distinct responsibilities rolled into one class. And each one introduces a separate reason for the class to change:

["If the scheduling system upgrades (e.g., moving to AI-based slot booking), this class changes.","If medical record regulations change (e.g., new government compliance rules), this class changes.","If the billing structure changes (e.g., adding a new insurance provider), this class changes.","If the ambulance dispatch logic changes (e.g., integrating GPS tracking), this class changes again."]
items: If the scheduling system upgrades (e.g., moving to AI-based slot booking), this class changes.
If medical record regulations change (e.g., new government compliance rules), this class changes.
If the billing structure changes (e.g., adding a new insurance provider), this class changes.
If the ambulance dispatch logic changes (e.g., integrating GPS tracking), this class changes again.

blocks.content: This class is tightly coupled to four different reasons to change. That's a red flag.
2. The Single Responsibility Principle
"A class should have one, and only one, reason to change."
Simple idea. Huge impact.
SRP is the "S" in SOLID and it's the first principle for a reason. It's the foundation everything else is built on.
But most people misunderstand it.
SRP is not about having fewer methods. It is not about keeping your class small. It is about ownership.
Ask yourself one question:
How many different reasons could force me to change this class?
If the answer is more than one your class has more than one responsibility.
One class. One job. One reason to change. That's it.
Real-World Analogy
Think of a smartphone. One device, but would you expect it to replace all of these?
["A professional DSLR camera","A dedicated GPS navigator","A desktop computer","A landline phone"]

Even though your phone can do all of it engineers still build each feature as a separate system internally. The camera chip doesn't interfere with the GPS module. The calling software doesn't touch the navigation logic.
Each component. One job. Zero overlap.
Your code should work the exact same way.
3. Why Does SRP Matter?
Easier to understand Walk into any class and instantly know what it does. No guessing, no digging, no surprises buried on line 347.
Easier to test One responsibility means one thing to verify. You can test billing logic without spinning up a notification service or touching a database.
Less risky to change Fix one thing, break nothing else. When responsibilities are separated, a change in your SMS provider won't somehow corrupt your payment records.
Built to reuse A focused class fits anywhere. A standalone InvoiceGenerator can serve your web app, your mobile app, and your internal dashboard without dragging along unrelated baggage.
Teams don't collide Different teams can work on different classes simultaneously without overwriting each other's logic or causing unexpected conflicts.
The longer a project lives, the more these benefits matter. SRP codebases age gracefully. God Class codebases become graveyards.
4. Applying SRP
Time to fix our HospitalSystem Class. The fix is straightforward stop forcing one class to serve four masters. Give each responsibility its own home.
["Checking doctor availability is one responsibility.","Maintaining patient records is another.","Calculating billing is another.","Dispatching ambulances is yet another."]
items: Checking doctor availability is one responsibility.

blocks.content: Each one deserves its own focused, well-named class. Let's walk through each one.
The Core: Patient Class
Let's start by extracting a simple Patient data class. Its only job is to represent a patient.
This class now does one thing: represent a patient. It does not calculate bills, dispatch ambulances, or store records. That is the job of others.
Responsibility 1: Doctor Availability
This class handles just the logic of checking and managing doctor schedules.

codes.python:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta


class AppointmentScheduler:
    """Handles just the logic of checking and managing doctor schedules."""

    def check_availability(self, doctor_id, date):
        if date < datetime.now():
            raise ValueError("Cannot book a past date")
        # Fetch doctor schedule and verify slot
        print(f"Checking availability for doctor: {doctor_id}")
        return True  # Simplified for illustration


if __name__ == "__main__":
    scheduler = AppointmentScheduler()
    future = datetime.now() + timedelta(days=1)
    available = scheduler.check_availability("DOC-101", future)
    print(f"Available: {available}")

blocks.content: If the scheduling system upgrades to AI-based slot booking, we only update this class. Nothing else is affected.
Responsibility 2: Patient Records
The responsibility for managing medical history belongs here.
You can change compliance rules, switch database providers, or restructure medical records entirely without touching the rest of the system.
Responsibility 3: Billing
This class handles the calculation of hospital charges.
You can add new insurance providers, change tax rules, or introduce dynamic pricing without affecting scheduling, records, or emergency logic. Billing is completely isolated.
Responsibility 4: Emergency Dispatch
This class is responsible only for handling ambulance dispatch.
It does not touch billing or medical records. It just handles emergencies. If you integrate live GPS tracking or a new dispatch algorithm, this is the only class you touch.
5. Common Pitfalls While Applying SRP
SRP sounds simple on paper. But in real projects, developers fall into the same traps over and over. Here are the most common mistakes and how to avoid them.
1. Splitting Too Much

Not every line of code deserves its own class. Some developers go overboard and create AppointmentDateValidator, DoctorIdChecker, SlotAvailabilityVerifier, and ScheduleConflictDetector when a single AppointmentScheduler would have been perfectly fine.
More classes does not mean better design. It means more files, more imports, more mental overhead, and a codebase that feels like a maze.
Group logic that changes together and belongs together. Cohesion matters as much as separation.
2. Mistaking Methods for Responsibilities
Consider a NotificationService that handles multiple alert types:

A developer might split this into AppointmentReminderSender and BillingAlertSender. But both methods share the same core responsibility sending notifications. Splitting them just creates unnecessary boilerplate with zero real benefit.
If methods serve the same business purpose, they belong in the same class.
3. Ignoring SRP in Small Utility Classes
blocks.text: 3. Ignoring SRP in Small Utility Classes

blocks.content: Small classes feel harmless. So developers let them grow unchecked. Consider:

Formatting logic changes when the report template changes. Upload logic changes when the cloud provider switches. Notification logic changes when the messaging system upgrades. Three independent reasons to change silently bundled into one "harmless" utility class.
Apply SRP early. Small classes become God Classes gradually, not overnight.
4. Misreading "Reason to Change
This is the most dangerous pitfall because it feels logical on the surface.
A common bad interpretation: "Only the hospital admin ever asks me to update this class, so it has one reason to change."

Wrong. SRP is not about who requests the change. It is about what kind of change is being made. If your PatientRecordService also handles billing calculations, it has two distinct responsibilities even if the same manager asks for both updates on the same day.
Ask the right question: Are these concerns cohesive, or are unrelated behaviors just sharing the same file?
6. Common Questions About SRP
"Doesn't this create too many small classes?"
blocks.text: "Doesn't this create too many small classes?"

blocks.content: Yes. And that's fine.
More classes does not mean more complexity. It means complexity is organized. Each class is easier to read, test, and reuse. You're not adding confusion you're containing it.
"How small should a responsibility be?"
Here's a simple test:
If you need the word "and" to describe your class, it has too many responsibilities.
"This class schedules appointments and sends notifications." Split it.
"Does SRP apply beyond classes?"
Absolutely. SRP works at every level:
["Method do one thing","Class have one reason to change","Module own one area of functionality","Service serve one domain"]
It's a mindset, not just a class-level rule.
"Does SRP make testing easier?"
Much easier. When a class does one thing, you test one thing. No mocking half the system. No worrying about hidden side effects. Just clean, focused test cases.
"What if responsibilities are related?"

Related is fine. A NotificationService that sends appointment reminders, billing alerts, and discharge summaries that's one responsibility. But the moment it starts generating PDFs or updating records, split it up.
"Is SRP just another rule?"
No. Think of it as a tool for managing change.
When something breaks, SRP limits the blast radius. When requirements shift, SRP tells you exactly where to go. Use it wisely, not blindly.
